blocks.x: If Widow’s Bay had added a kraken to its menagerie of the monstrous and the ghoulish, it might’ve looked something like Below. Like that Apple TV breakout, this taut Netflix miniseries captures the quirky personalities of a remote island community, but intertwines them with Lovecraftian monsters from the deep for a clever creature feature that launches a tale of climate change and corporate greed from a rock-solid dock of cultural authenticity. Anchored by a strong Josh Hartnett performance, it’s a show with a message that also never forgets to be goofily entertaining and memorably quirky. Creator Jesse McKeown values his characters as much as their predicament, leading to six episodes that make for a fun hang, even if their relative briefness leaves you wanting more. Then again, in the age of streaming bloat, a Netflix series that’s not only free of the typical plot sag but mostly shot in the bright sunlight feels as rare and awe-inspiring as the mysterious aquatic lifeforms at the center of Below.

Hartnett stars as Calvin Penney, an ice harvester in the Newfoundland village of Snook’s Arm, a real place off the coast of Canada that was resettled in 2018. Below opens with a young Calvin watching the Penney family home being moved across the water from one seaside location to another, only for it to get caught on something. His dad jumps from the boat to the floating abode, a choice that ends in a tragedy that will haunt Calvin for decades. Years later, and struggling to make ends meet due to the impact of climate change and pollution, Calvin’s latest haul seems dirty and somehow off, hinting at something unusual happening in the waters off Snook’s Arm. This catches the attention of a local scientist named Fonda Howander (Mackenzie Davis), who begins to examine what almost appears like a new amoebic presence in the ice. And that’s all before a massive iceberg appears on the horizon.

McKeown and his writers populate Snook’s Arm with memorable characters, most of them related to Calvin. There’s his supportive and headstrong sister Ruth, played by Newfoundlander Willow Kean, who adds some welcome local flavor to a cast who put on some entertaining but broad Canadian accents that sound like most of their research consisted of watching multiple episodes of Shoresy. There’s also the next generation of Penneys: Calvin’s daughter Mary (Ruby Stokes) and his sons Jay (Rohan Campbell) and Wade (Charlie Heaton). They all get subplots impacted by the main arc of the show, including a love interest who Mary brings home to meet the family and some debts that could get Jay in physical trouble. Of course, Stranger Things vet Heaton gets the most screen time, and he leans into a very different role than the one that made him famous, playing Wade as a goofy risk-taker who probably wouldn’t give soft-spoken Hawkins loner Jonathan Byers the time of day.

Early on, ice harvesting and local criminals take a back seat to an underwater kaiju, as the show really commits to its B-movie DNA. Before you know it, Calvin is on a submersible led by a team trying to track down the creature in a midsection that layers one surprise on top of another. Below often goes left when other programs would go right, especially in an extended interlude on an island even more remote that Snook’s Arm, where McKeown and company deftly weave together regional history, strong character work, and commentary on man’s relationship to the unknown.

Importantly, McKeown draws on his influences without ever turning Below into a cheap knockoff. If one looks deep into its waters, they can see the ineptitude of leadership in Jaws, the shrouded atmosphere of The Fog, and even a bit of J-horror in a mysterious, black-haired, waterlogged female figure who begins to haunt one of the characters. What is her connection to the tentacled beast beneath the waves? Below brilliantly alternates questions and answers, clearing away early mysteries to make room for the ones that will lure viewers to the miniseries’ conclusion. In an era of extreme over-exposition, this is the rare Netflix original that demands attention and rewards it, getting more done in six episodes than many of the streamer’s series have accomplished in multiple seasons.

As such, there are aspects of Below that wind up feeling too rushed. The finale speeds through so much plot and resolution that one wishes it was given a little more time to breathe. It’s a sprint to the finish line that requires some unfortunate, overwritten underlining of the show’s themes.

But the show’s flaws are easy to overlook thanks to its atmosphere, creature chaos, and Hartnett’s grounded lead performance. Extending a comeback that’s included Oppenheimer, Trap, and recent box-office champion Verity, the one-time teen heartthrob does some of the best work of his career in Below, giving Calvin relatability and urgency. He doesn’t overplay the trauma of a character who lost his dad in such extraordinary circumstances, and finds routes to convey Calvin’s inherent decency through action instead of direct dialogue. He’s so often the audience surrogate in this otherworldly tale; that Hartnett makes us believe he’s being terrorized by a gigantic cryptid is ultimately even more essential to Below’s success than its top-notch creature effects.

When Netflix’s competitors are turning to familiar IP like Carrie and Friday The 13th to bring subscribers in this Halloween, it’s refreshing to watch something like Below, which feels both familiar in its influences and original in its use of specific setting, character, and atmosphere. It may not be a runaway creative success like Widow’s Bay, but it’s another reminder that horror often works best when it’s grounded in believable, eccentric corners of the world.
